title: The Effects of Lighting Design on Mood, Attention, and Stress
research_question: To compare the effects of three lighting conditions (bright white SAD light, dim 450nm blue light, and dim warm control light) on mood, sustained attention, and physiological stress.

participants.description: 19-22-year-old students from Reed College (6 female, 2 non-binary, 2 non-binary women, 2 male). One participant excluded due to incomplete data. Participants with color deficiencies were excluded. 27% met minimum requirements for possible SAD.
participants.recruitment: social media posts and word of mouth

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three lighting conditions: 1) Light therapy (SAD): 10,000 lux, 6500°K, full-spectrum white light. 2) Blue light: 40 lux, 450 nm light. 3) Control light: 40 lux, 3500°K standard office light (warm incandescent). Participants spent 45 minutes in each condition.

measures.instrument: Heart Rate (measured at pre-session, mid-session, post-session)
Seasonal Pattern Assessment Questionnaire (SPAQ) - shortened version

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: change in reported Total Mood Disturbance (POMS-SF)
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Total Mood Disturbance was not significantly different across light condition, F(2, 10) = 0.55, p = .58.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Depression-Dejection was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.089, p =.92.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.mechanism: Blue light should have reduced melatonin production and fatigue, but did not show statistically significant effect.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Fatigue was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.14, p= .34.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session (T2-T1)
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,9) = 1.49, p= .25.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: change in heart rate from pre-session to post-session (T3-T1)
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heat rate pre-session to post-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.044, p= .96.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: average reaction time in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized that bright SAD lamps would distract and irritate participants, leading to slower reaction times.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that average reaction time during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.34, p = .28.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: standard deviation of reaction times in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Large variances in response time indicate waxing and waning of attention.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that the standard deviation of reaction times during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.18, p= .33.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: percentage of omission errors in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Increased omission errors in SAD condition indicate participants were unable to commit full attention to the task.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that omission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.5, p=.62.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux white; Control: 40 lux warm; Blue: 40 lux 450nm)
findings.consequent: percentage of commission errors in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Possible difficulty with color discrimination in blue light condition due to after-image.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that commission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.9, p=.42.

mechanisms: Blue light impacts intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells, sending signals to the superchiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, affecting melatonin secretion and circadian rhythms.
Bright lights can be too distracting and uncomfortable, negatively influencing cognitive functions like attention and increasing physiological agitation (heart rate).
implementation_implications: Further research is needed to understand the effects of blue light from devices on mood and sleep cycles to avoid dysregulation.
Lighting can be modulated in offices and schools to increase productivity for specific tasks.
Dim, warm lighting may promote relaxation and reduce fidgeting/aggression in classrooms.
Brighter lights may promote self-awareness and reflection.
Small amendments to lighting design, such as switching lightbulbs, can change comfort levels in workspaces.
limitations: Small sample size (N=11) leading to insufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences.
Variability in weather patterns (snow, sun) during data collection, potentially influencing mood/stress and increasing data variation.

Participants completed sessions at various times of day, potentially obscuring stronger effects that might be evident in the evening (especially for blue light's impact on circadian rhythms/melatonin).
Variations in participants' academic workload and sleep patterns across the semester (normal week, midterms, spring break) could have affected stress levels and data quality.
The CCPT might not measure the specific type of attention affected by lighting conditions (e.g., multitasking or suppressing distraction might be more relevant).

The POMS-SF might not be sensitive enough to detect minor mood changes, or some subscales (Confusion, Anger) might be irrelevant. Participants found some adjectives synonymous or unfamiliar ('Bushed').
Participants might have remembered and tried to maintain consistency with their previous POMS-SF responses.
Heart rate might not fully capture physiological arousal as precisely as skin conductance or cortisol, and was easily influenced by the researcher's presence.
The study's findings might represent a genuine null effect, implying previous literature on lighting effects could be exaggerated due to methodological issues.
Subjective opinions and personal preferences for certain lighting conditions might have influenced participants' emotional states, skewing results.
The sample did not predominantly include participants with SAD, which might limit the detectability of mood, attention, and stress changes.

instruments_used.name: POMS-SF
instruments_used.description: Profile of Mood States - Short Form
